Antioxidants are widely discussed as potentially protective, but the evidence is mixed. Some sources argue that diets rich in antioxidant-containing foods (e.g., fruits, vegetables, whole foods) may reduce cancer risk by lowering oxidative stress and inflammation [d1,d3,d4,d6,d9]. However, large randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews report no benefit of antioxidant supplements for primary cancer prevention and even suggest possible harm, including worse outcomes in some patients and increased prostate cancer risk with high-dose vitamin E [d2,d7,d8,d10].

Given the conflicting clinical and observational findings, there is no definitive consensus that antioxidants prevent cancer. The strongest high-credibility evidence indicates no proven benefit from supplements and potential risks, while food-based antioxidants remain plausibly beneficial but unproven for cancer prevention.
